newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Signs of progress on NATO, Chechnya boost Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Signs of progress on NATO, Chechnya boost Yeltsin.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was boosted on Sunday by glimmers of progress at talks with separatists in Chechnya and with NATO over its eastward expansion plans.
Russian and Chechen negotiators reported movement at talks in the rebel region and said they hoped to sign a political agreement, amounting to a formal peace declaration, in the next eight days.

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, briefing Yeltsin on a week of talks in Western Europe, said differences remained over NATO's plans to take in former communist-ruled countries from eastern Europe but there were also signs of progress.
"In the minister's opinion, talks made progress in several areas," the presidential press office said in a statement released after Primakov met Yeltsin at the Gorky-9 state residence outside Moscow.
"But negotiations with NATO are not like travelling along a wide avenue," the statement quoted Primakov as saying.

During a European tour last week which included talks with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, Primakov said repeatedly that Russia remained firmly opposed to the Western defence alliance's plans to expand eastwards.
Russia says the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's enlargement would threaten its security, open new divisions in Europe and open Yeltsin to attack by his political foes.

But Western diplomats said after Primakov's latest talks that Moscow now appeared determined to clinch some sort of deal before a NATO summit in Madrid in July at which the alliance will invite some former Warsaw Pact countries to join.
Negotiations are focused on a document that will govern post-Cold War ties between NATO and Moscow, although the alliance opposes Russia's demands to make it legally binding.

NATO expansion is likely to dominate a summit meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki on March 20-21. Yeltsin ordered Primakov to go to Washington to complete preparations for the meeting but the Kremlin did not say when he would go.

Failure to win concessions over NATO expansion would be ammunition for Yeltsin's political opponents and further dent his authority after the health problems which kept him out of the Kremlin for the best part of eight months.
The 66-year-old Kremlin leader would face similar problems if talks on relations with Chechnya went badly.
The two sides remain firmly entrenched over Chechnya's independence demands, which prompted a 21-month conflict that killed tens of thousands of people.
Russia rules out secession, but Chechen leaders say the region is already independent.
Despite their differences, Russian and Chechen negotiators said they had had fruitful talks in the Chechen capital Grozny.
"Centuries-old confrontation, of which there have been relapses every now and then, is coming to an end," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Russian negotiator Ivan Rybkin as saying.

Completion of a political agreement, and a series of agreements on economic issues, would help increase trust and reassure each side that the other is sincere in its efforts to work out a way to live togther in peace.

Yeltsin gave no indication at the weekend about who he would replace in a cabinet reshuffle expected this week after he criticised the government's failure to pay wages on time and the slow progress of military reform.

Defence Minister Igor Rodionov is the focus of some of the rumours. Interfax news agency said he had cancelled a planned trip to Georgia this week but the defence ministry in Moscow said it had no information on the reported cancellation.
